summary: The state of Qin conquered its last rivals in 221 BCE and its king became the First Emperor, standardising script, coinage and law, but the dynasty collapsed in revolts soon after his death and ended in 206 BCE. Liu Bang founded the Han in 202 BCE; under Emperor Wu (141–87 BCE) it drove back the Xiongnu and expanded into Central Asia, Korea and the far south. After Wang Mang's Xin interlude (9–23 CE) the Eastern Han ruled from Luoyang until rebellion and warlords ended it in 220 CE.

details: For centuries the Warring States had fought for supremacy while the old Zhou kings faded into figureheads, and Qin, secure in the mountain-ringed Guanzhong basin in the west, had built the most efficient army and state. From 230 BCE King Zheng conquered the six remaining states one by one: Han, Zhao, Yan, Wei, Chu and finally Qi, whose capital Linzi fell in 221 BCE. He took the new title Shi Huangdi, 'First Emperor', and governed through appointed officials instead of royal relatives. For the first time the Chinese heartland, from the Yellow River plains to the Yangtze, was a single empire.

Xiongnu herders in the Ordos, the grassland inside the great northern loop of the Yellow River, often raided Qin farmers. The First Emperor sent General Meng Tian north with an army said to number 300,000, and in 215 BCE he expelled the Xiongnu from the Ordos and drove them back onto the Mongolian Plateau. Qin settled farmers in the region and began the long chain of defences later remembered as the Great Wall. The empire's northern frontier now enclosed the Ordos, but after Qin fell the Xiongnu leader Modu retook it.

Obsessed with immortality, the First Emperor died in 210 BCE while touring the eastern frontier, reportedly while seeking an elixir of eternal life. His chief eunuch Zhao Gao and chancellor Li Si hid his death, forged an order telling the heir, Prince Fusu, to kill himself, and had General Meng Tian put to death. They placed a younger son, Huhai, on the throne as the Second Emperor, hoping to rule through him. Huhai's purges, building projects and higher taxes soon set off revolts across the empire, and the newly united realm began to break apart.

Rebellions spread from 209 BCE, and rebel leaders declared themselves kings of the old states. In 207 BCE Zhao Gao forced the Second Emperor to kill himself and installed Ziying, who ruled only as a king; Ziying had Zhao Gao killed but, after just 46 days, surrendered to the rebel general Liu Bang when he reached the capital, Xianyang. The Chu leader Xiang Yu then had Ziying executed and Xianyang destroyed in 206 BCE. The Qin dynasty ended after only 15 years, and its empire split into some eighteen rival kingdoms.

After Qin fell, Xiang Yu of Chu made himself overlord and gave Liu Bang, a man of humble birth, the small fief of Hanzhong. War between the two, the Chu–Han Contention, followed for four years. In the winter of 203–202 BCE Liu Bang's armies trapped Xiang Yu at Gaixia and destroyed his army, and Xiang Yu killed himself by the Wu River. A few months later Liu Bang proclaimed himself emperor of a new dynasty named Han, after his old fief; with one brief break, it would rule China for four centuries.

Modu Chanyu had united the Xiongnu into a powerful steppe empire, and when a Han vassal king, Xin, defected to him, they captured Jinyang in the north. Emperor Gaozu led a large army to drive them back, but near Pingcheng (modern Datong) he and his vanguard were surrounded on Mount Baideng and cut off for seven days. He escaped, reportedly after his envoys persuaded Modu's wife to urge a withdrawal. In 198 BCE the Han agreed the heqin treaty, sending a princess and gifts of silk, food and wine, and until the 130s BCE they bought peace on the northern frontier rather than fighting.

Liu Bang had given his relatives large semi-independent kingdoms covering a third to a half of the empire, and by the 150s BCE princes such as Liu Pi of Wu minted coins, collected taxes and largely ignored the court. When Emperor Jing, advised by Chao Cuo, began cutting their lands, seven kings rose in revolt in 154 BCE. The imperial general Zhou Yafu let the loyal kingdom of Liang absorb the rebel attack while his cavalry cut their supply lines, and the revolt was crushed within three months. The kingdoms were reduced and imperial power grew sharply, preparing the way for Emperor Wu's expansion.

After years of Han offensives under Emperor Wu, the Xiongnu chanyu Yizhixie pulled his people north of the Gobi Desert, hoping the barren land would protect them. In early 119 BCE Wu sent two columns of 50,000 cavalry each, backed by over 140,000 infantry and supply troops, across the desert under Wei Qing and Huo Qubing. Wei Qing routed the chanyu's army in a sandstorm, while Huo Qubing crushed the eastern Xiongnu and pushed far north, reportedly as far as Lake Baikal. The Xiongnu lost much of their manpower and livestock and were driven from the lands south of the Gobi, though Han lost some 80 per cent of its horses in a decade of war.

As Qin collapsed, Zhao Tuo, a former Qin officer, had set himself up as king of Nanyue, covering modern Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam. In 113 BCE Nanyue's queen dowager, herself Chinese, proposed accepting Han overlordship, but the minister Lü Jia led the opposition and in 112 BCE had her executed. Emperor Wu sent six armies by sea, overland and down the Xi River, and in 111 BCE the capital Panyu (modern Guangzhou) fell and Nanyue surrendered. Han set up nine commanderies there, pushing its southern frontier to northern Vietnam and opening sea trade with Southeast Asia.

Wiman Chosŏn, the kingdom of Gojoseon in northern Korea and southern Manchuria, under King Ugeo blocked envoys from other Korean chiefs from reaching the Han court. In 109 BCE Emperor Wu invaded with two forces: 50,000 men by sea across the Bohai and another army overland through Liaodong. Both suffered early defeats, and the capital Wanggeom (near modern Pyongyang) held out for months. In 108 BCE leading ministers surrendered and King Ugeo was assassinated, and Han created four commanderies in the northern half of the peninsula. The most important, Lelang, remained under Chinese control until 313 CE.

After the wars with the Xiongnu, Han wanted to control the oasis kingdoms of the Tarim Basin, both to keep the Xiongnu away from China and to command the Silk Road trade that passed through them. In 60 or 59 BCE, after a Xiongnu prince, the Rizhu King, submitted to Han, the envoy Zheng Ji was made Protector-General of the Western Regions, overseeing both the northern and southern routes from a headquarters at Wulei near Kucha. It was the first direct rule by a Chinese government in the region. Han power now reached deep into what is today Xinjiang.

In the last decades of the Western Han, the family of Empress Dowager Wang held the regency for a series of weak or child emperors. Her nephew Wang Mang became regent in 1 BCE and acting emperor for the infant heir Ruzi Ying in 6 CE, then in 9 CE claimed the Mandate of Heaven and founded his own Xin dynasty. His reforms, such as outlawing slavery, sharing out land and issuing new coins, met fierce opposition, and huge Yellow River floods drove peasants into rebel bands such as the Red Eyebrows. In 23 CE rebels stormed Chang'an and killed him, and Han control of the Tarim Basin was lost.

Liu Xiu, a distant descendant of the Han emperors, was one of several claimants who rose during the civil wars after Wang Mang's fall. He proclaimed himself emperor on 5 August 25 CE, taking the name Guangwu, and defeated the marauding Red Eyebrows and rival warlords, reunifying China by 36 CE. He made Luoyang, about 335 km east of the ruined Chang'an, his capital, which is why his dynasty is called the Eastern Han. His reforms gave the Han nearly two more centuries of rule over a restored empire.

By the 180s CE the Eastern Han court was paralysed by power struggles, while peasants suffered heavy taxes and forced labour. The Taoist faith healer Zhang Jue built a vast following, the Way of Supreme Peace, and when his plot was betrayed the rising broke out early, in 184 CE, across eight provinces; the rebels wore yellow headscarves. Han armies crushed the main revolt within a year, but smaller uprisings went on until 205. Many generals raised to fight the rebels kept their troops and became warlords, and the empire's central authority never recovered.

After 189 CE the warlord Dong Zhuo wrecked the Han court, and the empire split among rival warlords. Cao Cao took control of the young Emperor Xian in 196 and ruled in his name, but his drive to reunify China was stopped at the Battle of Red Cliffs in 208–209. In 220 his son Cao Pi pressured Emperor Xian to abdicate and founded the Wei dynasty, formally ending the Han. Liu Bei proclaimed the Shu Han dynasty in 221 and Sun Quan founded Wu in 222, so China was divided into the Three Kingdoms until 280.
